tpe-sebs.title: Instrument socket dust plug
tpe-sebs.use: Cap an unused instrument opening with a flexible pull-tab plug.
tpe-sebs.why: The rubbery SEBS body can compress into a shaped opening, and a flexible pull tab permits repeated removal without needing a separate hinge or rigid latch.
tpe-sebs.advantage: The compliant plug can follow an irregular opening and permit removal through a flexible pull tab.
tpe-sebs.tradeoff: Repeated rubbing can wear this elastomer faster than the TPU comparisons, and the plug does not establish electrical or environmental protection.

tpu-85a.title: Flextail device stand
tpu-85a.use: The documented FLEXTAIL stand uses TPU 85A for its flexible body.
tpu-85a.why: The soft elastomer can conform around the device and deform during installation; this provides an engineering reason to evaluate the grade, while the creator evidence establishes only the actual material use.
tpu-85a.advantage: The soft stand can deform around the device during fitting and provide compliant contact underneath it.
tpu-85a.tradeoff: Soft TPU creeps under sustained load, so check the cradle fit and stability over time.

tpu-85a.title: Cable-bend protective boot
tpu-85a.use: Fit a soft bend-limiting boot behind a low-voltage cable connector.
tpu-85a.why: TPU 85A can bend repeatedly and stretch around a connector, allowing a thin printed boot to spread the bend over a longer region rather than create one sharp kink.
tpu-85a.advantage: The flexible boot can distribute cable curvature instead of presenting a sharp rigid edge at the connector.
tpu-85a.tradeoff: The boot needs pull and flex testing; soft material alone does not prove cable fatigue life or strain-relief effectiveness.

tpu-85a.title: Low-load transport-roller sleeve
tpu-85a.use: Fit a compliant sleeve to a small bench transport roller.
tpu-85a.why: Soft TPU deforms at the contact patch and offers published abrasion data, making it a candidate for moving lightweight items without a fully rigid contact surface.
tpu-85a.advantage: The compliant sleeve can form a wider low-force contact patch than a rigid roller surface.
tpu-85a.tradeoff: Sustained roller pressure can flatten the sleeve, and grip depends on surface texture and the transported material.

tpu-85a.title: Gripper cup for irregular housings
tpu-85a.use: Create replaceable compliant contact cups for handling small plastic housings.
tpu-85a.why: TPU 85A can deform around an irregular surface and recover through repeated motion, helping a gripper contact more than a few rigid points at modest force.
tpu-85a.advantage: The compliant cups can distribute a modest gripping load across more of an irregular housing surface.
tpu-85a.tradeoff: The cups can shift the effective locating position under load, so measure actual grip force and repeatability.

tpu-85a.title: Reusable equipment cable strap
tpu-85a.use: Bundle a light cable harness with a stretchable printed strap.
tpu-85a.why: High elongation and repeated-flex capability support a strap that bends around the bundle and stretches over a locating peg without a separate rigid hinge.
tpu-85a.advantage: The flexible strap can wrap tightly around the harness without requiring a separate mechanical hinge.
tpu-85a.tradeoff: Constant tension relaxes through creep, so use a positive latch and avoid relying on stretch alone for retention.

tpu-95a.title: Decorated Galaxy A07 phone case
tpu-95a.use: The documented Samsung Galaxy A07 case is printed in TPU 95A.
tpu-95a.why: The elastomer can stretch around the phone and recover around corners, offering a plausible reason for this material choice; the photographed finish also includes painting and decoration.
tpu-95a.advantage: The elastic shell can fit over corners and retain the phone through flexible edge engagement.
tpu-95a.tradeoff: The source demonstrates a build, not certified drop protection, and thin edges or decorations can fail first.

tpu-95a.title: Indoor robot tyre
tpu-95a.use: Fit a replaceable flexible tyre to a rigid indoor robot wheel.
tpu-95a.why: TPU 95A combines elastic deformation with documented abrasion resistance, making it a useful middle-ground candidate between a soft 85A tread and a firmer hard-TPU wheel.
tpu-95a.advantage: The flexible abrasion-resistant contact ring can deform around small surface irregularities during indoor robot movement.
tpu-95a.tradeoff: Grip is surface-dependent, and constant load can deform the tyre; test rolling resistance and shape after storage.

tpu-95a.title: Low-pressure enclosure gasket prototype
tpu-95a.use: Print a removable gasket for checking the fit of a small enclosure lid.
tpu-95a.why: Elastic TPU can compress between the lid and body, allowing the gasket profile and fastening pattern to be evaluated before choosing a final sealing method.
tpu-95a.advantage: The compressible gasket can accommodate small mating-surface variations while the lid applies a controlled clamping force.
tpu-95a.tradeoff: Layer paths can leak and sustained compression creeps, so the print has no assumed waterproof or pressure rating.

tpu-95a.title: Flexible cable-guide elbow
tpu-95a.use: Route a cable around a tight equipment corner using a compliant elbow.
tpu-95a.why: TPU 95A can flex during installation while retaining a more substantial shape than very soft grades, and repeated-flex capability makes it worth evaluating for occasional cable movement.
tpu-95a.advantage: The compliant guide can yield during cable installation while retaining a more defined path than very soft TPU.
tpu-95a.tradeoff: The elbow must not force the cable below its allowed bend radius, and constant deflection can relax the fit.

tpu-95a.title: Replaceable equipment-edge bumper
tpu-95a.use: Fit a removable TPU bumper to an exposed instrument-enclosure edge.
tpu-95a.why: The elastic grade can deform on incidental contact instead of presenting a fully rigid edge, while its abrasion data supports evaluation for repeated handling against a bench.
tpu-95a.advantage: The deformable bumper can soften incidental edge contact while presenting an abrasion-resistant, replaceable contact surface.
tpu-95a.tradeoff: No impact attenuation is quantified here, and sustained squeeze can loosen the slide-on channel through creep.

tpu-98a.title: Sim-racing brake-pedal spring
tpu-98a.use: The documented T-LCM modification uses a printed spring in Extrudr 98A TPU.
tpu-98a.why: Hard TPU remains flexible enough to deform while holding a firmer shape than softer elastomers, making geometry and hardness useful variables for a simulator pedal's resistance.
tpu-98a.advantage: The firm elastomer can provide deformable pedal resistance while recovering through the simulator's normal travel.
tpu-98a.tradeoff: This is a gaming pedal, and creep can change resistance over time; check travel and return repeatedly.

tpu-98a.title: Low-load timing-belt prototype
tpu-98a.use: Print a short belt for a guarded, low-load mechanism demonstration.
tpu-98a.why: Hard TPU combines repeated-flex capability with a firmer body than soft elastomers, allowing tooth geometry and routing to be explored while the belt bends around small pulleys.
tpu-98a.advantage: The firm flexible belt can wrap around pulleys while holding tooth shape better than very soft TPU.
tpu-98a.tradeoff: The print has no tensile-cord reinforcement or power-transmission rating; inspect tooth deformation, creep and layer separation during testing.

tpu-98a.title: Instrument trolley wheel tread
tpu-98a.use: Fit a firm replaceable tread around a small rigid trolley wheel.
tpu-98a.why: Hard TPU offers documented abrasion resistance and some compliance, making it a candidate where softer TPU would flatten excessively under a modest rolling load.
tpu-98a.advantage: The firm abrasion-resistant tread can offer some compliance without the large deformation of a softer elastomer.
tpu-98a.tradeoff: Constant load can still create a flat spot, so test parked deformation and rolling force at the intended load.

tpu-98a.title: Flexible accessory snap bracket
tpu-98a.use: Retain a lightweight removable accessory with a thick, slightly flexible bracket.
tpu-98a.why: Hard TPU can deform enough for installation while retaining its shape more firmly than softer TPU, making it useful for a forgiving snap geometry rather than a rigid brittle latch.
tpu-98a.advantage: The firm elastomer can spread for installation and recover around an accessory without a brittle rigid latch.
tpu-98a.tradeoff: Repeated retention force can decrease through creep, so use a positive stop and measure the force after cycling.

tpu-98a.title: Bench feeder drive-wheel sleeve
tpu-98a.use: Fit a firm elastomer sleeve to a small materials-feeding demonstration wheel.
tpu-98a.why: Hard TPU has comparatively favorable abrasion data and enough flexibility to fit a hub, making it a candidate for a durable contact ring with controlled deformation.
tpu-98a.advantage: The firm wear-resistant sleeve can maintain a more defined feeding radius than a very soft contact ring.
tpu-98a.tradeoff: Traction is not predicted by Shore hardness; check slip, surface marking and sustained-compression deformation with the actual feedstock.

pp-cf.title: Lightweight chemical-apparatus splash baffle
pp-cf.use: Mount a shaped splash baffle around compatible bench fluid-handling equipment.
pp-cf.why: Carbon-filled PP combines very low moisture uptake with broad chemical resistance and relatively low density, making it a candidate where the baffle should not swell significantly in ordinary wet service.
pp-cf.advantage: The chemically resistant, low-moisture-uptake baffle can retain its function through repeated compatible splash exposure.
pp-cf.tradeoff: Check the exact chemical and temperature; this print is a splash-control concept, not a pressure-containing component.

pp-cf.title: Moving-toolhead cable duct
pp-cf.use: Route a cable bundle through a light duct on a moving toolhead.
pp-cf.why: The PP composite's low density limits added moving mass, while low moisture uptake and published thermal-deflection data support evaluation around warm, humid equipment.
pp-cf.advantage: The low-density duct can reduce the mass carried by the moving toolhead while resisting moisture uptake.
pp-cf.tradeoff: Large thin PP parts can warp, and the carbon-filled material should not be assumed electrically insulating.

pp-cf.title: Wash-area sensor mounting cover
pp-cf.use: Locate a sensor behind a splash-facing cover on noncritical workshop equipment.
pp-cf.why: Low water uptake helps the PP matrix resist moisture-driven dimensional changes, and its chemical resistance supports evaluation around compatible cleaning solutions after checking the particular formulation.
pp-cf.advantage: The low-moisture-uptake mount can preserve fit through repeated wetting with a validated compatible cleaning solution.
pp-cf.tradeoff: Chemical resistance does not make the assembly waterproof; seals, wiring and fasteners need their own validation.

pp-cf.title: Chemical-container rim support bracket
pp-cf.use: Support a lightweight removable accessory on the rim of a compatible chemical container.
pp-cf.why: The reinforced PP matrix combines chemical resistance and limited water uptake, making it a candidate where ordinary moisture-sensitive nylon fixtures would change properties during repeated exposure.
pp-cf.advantage: The chemically resistant bracket can retain its role around compatible splashes without nylon-like moisture conditioning changes.
pp-cf.tradeoff: Do not infer pressure or lifting capability; check the container material, fluid and actual clamp load together.

pp-cf.title: Warm-air instrument duct adapter
pp-cf.use: Join two nonstandard low-pressure warm-air duct openings on a bench instrument.
pp-cf.why: The low-density PP composite reduces adapter mass, and its published loaded heat-deflection data provides a starting point for evaluating a warm duct connection.
pp-cf.advantage: The lightweight, thermally resistant adapter can limit added duct mass while maintaining shape at a validated temperature.
pp-cf.tradeoff: HDT is not a continuous-service temperature, and shrinkage can distort the flange enough to prevent sealing.

pp-gf.title: Chemical-rinse parts basket prototype
pp-gf.use: Print a perforated basket for handling small parts in a compatible rinse bath.
pp-gf.why: Glass-filled PP offers rigid geometry with low water uptake and broad chemical resistance, making it a candidate where the basket should retain its shape during repeated wet handling.
pp-gf.advantage: The rigid, low-moisture-uptake basket can keep parts separated through repeated compatible wet-handling cycles.
pp-gf.tradeoff: The exact bath chemistry and temperature need compatibility checks, and the print is not a rated lifting basket.

pp-gf.title: Wash-area sensor protective cover
pp-gf.use: Cover a sensor mount against incidental splashes on noncritical workshop equipment.
pp-gf.why: The rigid glass-filled PP matrix combines low moisture uptake and chemical resistance, making it useful to evaluate where a flexible unfilled PP cover would not hold its shape.
pp-gf.advantage: The stiff, low-moisture-uptake cover can maintain clearance around the sensor through compatible splash exposure.
pp-gf.tradeoff: A printed cover does not establish waterproofing, and PP shrinkage can distort a large mounting flange.

pp-gf.title: Chemical-process assembly locating nest
pp-gf.use: Locate a small compatible component during an ordinary wet assembly operation.
pp-gf.why: Glass reinforcement stiffens the PP body, while low moisture uptake helps reduce humidity-driven changes and the PP matrix tolerates many chemicals after specific compatibility checking.
pp-gf.advantage: The rigid fixture can maintain locating features in wet conditions without large moisture-driven property changes.
pp-gf.tradeoff: Layered surfaces may retain residue, and chemical compatibility alone does not establish cleanliness or dimensional accuracy.

pp-gf.title: Warm-air duct mounting flange
pp-gf.use: Fasten a lightweight duct transition to a warm bench instrument.
pp-gf.why: The glass-filled PP is rigid and has published loaded heat-deflection data, making it a candidate for a shaped flange where unfilled PP would flex too readily.
pp-gf.advantage: The stiff, thermally resistant flange can maintain duct alignment at a validated warm operating condition.
pp-gf.tradeoff: Thermal deflection data is not a continuous-use rating, and warping can compromise the flat mating surface.

pp-gf.title: Wet-equipment cable-routing raceway
pp-gf.use: Route low-voltage sensor cables through a rigid channel beside compatible wet equipment.
pp-gf.why: Glass-filled PP provides a firm channel while its low moisture uptake and chemical resistance support evaluation around ordinary damp conditions and compatible cleaning agents.
pp-gf.advantage: The rigid channel can keep cables separated in damp service without substantial water-absorption changes.
pp-gf.tradeoff: Do not assume an electrical insulation rating, and verify that the chosen cleaner does not attack the actual filament formulation.

pe.title: Chemical-workbench drip tray prototype
pe.use: Print a shallow removable tray for incidental drips from compatible bench containers.
pe.why: The cataloged HDPE filament combines low water uptake and broad chemical resistance, making it a candidate for a shaped tray after checking the exact liquid and formulation.
pe.advantage: The chemically resistant, low-moisture-uptake tray can tolerate compatible drips without substantial water-absorption changes.
pe.tradeoff: Printed layers can leak, and this modified filament is not equivalent to plain molded HDPE or certified containment.

pe.title: Sliding-bin guide block
pe.use: Guide a lightweight storage bin with a replaceable shaped plastic block.
pe.why: The listed HDPE filament emphasizes abrasion and crack resistance, while its comparatively stiff modified formulation helps a small guide retain its geometry during light sliding contact.
pe.advantage: The abrasion-resistant modified polyethylene can provide a replaceable contact surface while its stiffness maintains the guiding shape.
pe.tradeoff: No friction or printed wear-life result is provided, so check the mating surface, debris and clearance experimentally.

pe.title: Packaging-cap fit prototype
pe.use: Prototype a closure outline for packaging intended to use HDPE in production.
pe.why: The polyethylene chemistry makes it useful for exploring basic packaging geometry, but the cataloged low-warp filament is modified and substantially stiffer than plain HDPE stock.
pe.advantage: The polyethylene-based prototype can reveal geometric fit issues while preserving an explicit distinction from production material behavior.
pe.tradeoff: This prototype cannot predict production squeeze behavior, sealing or food-contact suitability from the polymer name alone.

pe.title: Wash-area mechanism splash shield
pe.use: Cover a low-load mechanism against incidental splashes with a shaped removable shield.
pe.why: The HDPE filament has low water uptake and resistance to many compatible chemicals, while its modified stiffness supports a relatively firm shield instead of a floppy membrane.
pe.advantage: The stiff, low-moisture-uptake shield can maintain mechanism clearance through repeated compatible splashes.
pe.tradeoff: Compatibility must match the actual cleaner, and shrinkage can distort broad flat mounting faces.

pe.title: Lubricated demonstrator gear cover
pe.use: Enclose a small low-load gear demonstration with a removable HDPE cover.
pe.why: Resistance to many oils and low moisture uptake support evaluation around compatible lubricant, while the modified filament's stiffness helps the cover maintain clearance from the moving gears.
pe.advantage: The stiff, low-moisture-uptake cover can preserve gear clearance around incidental exposure to a compatible lubricant.
pe.tradeoff: It is a cover rather than a proven structural housing; verify lubricant compatibility, heat exposure and fastener fit.

pp.title: Pajero stereo adapter brackets
pp.use: The documented Pioneer stereo installation uses PP adapter brackets in a Mitsubishi Pajero.
pp.why: The creator explicitly selected PP for flexibility; its semi-flexible behavior allows a bracket to accommodate installation movement instead of acting like a rigid composite spacer.
pp.advantage: The flexible brackets can yield during installation instead of demanding the alignment of a rigid spacer.
pp.tradeoff: PP creeps under sustained load, so installed fit and fastener retention need checking over time.

pp.title: ECC2 toolhead front cover
pp.use: The documented ECC2 toolhead modification includes a front cover printed in PP.
pp.why: The material's low density and semi-flexible behavior make a removable cover a plausible application, while the creator evidence establishes the actual filament use rather than a tested engineering rationale.
pp.advantage: The lightweight, semi-flexible cover can yield during removal without adding a heavy rigid shell to the toolhead.
pp.tradeoff: The pictured bumper is ASA, not PP, and the PP cover needs clearance and heat testing on the machine.

pp.title: Living-hinge small-parts box
pp.use: Print a small parts box with a thin integral hinged lid.
pp.why: PP's repeated-flex capability and ductile behavior make it a candidate for a living hinge, where a reinforced rigid composite would place greater strain on a brittle thin section.
pp.advantage: The ductile hinge section can repeatedly bend while the thicker box walls retain their useful shape.
pp.tradeoff: Printed hinge life depends strongly on section thickness, orientation and processing; test repeated opening rather than assuming molded-PP performance.

pp.title: Flexible snap-lid prototype
pp.use: Prototype a small enclosure with a lid that flexes around locating clips.
pp.why: The semi-flexible PP body and high elongation permit bending during assembly, helping evaluate snap geometry for a product intended to use polypropylene in production.
pp.advantage: The ductile lid can flex during engagement instead of depending on a brittle latch surviving repeated bending.
pp.tradeoff: Printed shrinkage alters the latch fit, and sustained latch deflection can relax through creep.

pp.title: Chemical-workbench vial positioning rack
pp.use: Locate closed sample containers in a rack near compatible bench chemicals.
pp.why: PP combines low moisture uptake with resistance to many acids, alkalis and solvents, making it a candidate for a positioning rack exposed to incidental compatible splashes.
pp.advantage: The chemically resistant, low-moisture-uptake rack can retain its purpose through incidental compatible splashes.
pp.tradeoff: The rack is not certified containment, and the flexible material needs adequate ribs to prevent loaded shelves sagging.

pmma.title: LED light-bar diffuser
pmma.use: Print a removable cover over an indoor decorative LED strip.
pmma.why: PMMA is sold as a transparent glass substitute, making it a candidate when transmitting and spreading light matters more than structural loading; printed layers will scatter light rather than behave like polished optical acrylic.
pmma.advantage: Transmitted light can illuminate the cover while FDM texture helps soften the visible point-source pattern.
pmma.tradeoff: The catalog has no grade-specific thermal data, so heat exposure needs testing.

pmma.title: Instrument dial window
pmma.use: Print a shaped window for a low-stress indoor instrument mockup.
pmma.why: The acrylic chemistry and transparent-cover application make PMMA relevant when a viewer must see a dial through a custom curved opening; transparency depends on the filament, walls and finishing.
pmma.advantage: A light-transmitting cover allows the dial to remain visible through the shaped enclosure opening.
pmma.tradeoff: Do not assume optical clarity, impact resistance or a temperature rating from this sparse catalog entry.

pmma.title: Edge-lit nameplate insert
pmma.use: Print a translucent lettering insert that couples light from an LED base.
pmma.why: PMMA is identified for light guides, so a simple edge-lit display is a useful experiment in directing light through a shaped part; layer lines can deliberately provide visible scattering.
pmma.advantage: A light-transmitting insert can turn the lettering itself into the illuminated feature of the display.
pmma.tradeoff: Alcohol-based cleaners and oils can craze stressed acrylic, so cleaning compatibility matters.

pmma.title: Inspection cover for a display model
pmma.use: Print a removable cover that lets viewers inspect a model mechanism.
pmma.why: Acrylic is a candidate where the design needs a transparent barrier and little mechanical load; the goal is visibility rather than a protective machine guard or a load-bearing component.
pmma.advantage: The interior mechanism remains visible through a light-transmitting cover without removing it for every viewing.
pmma.tradeoff: Solvents such as acetone dissolve PMMA, and no printed strength data is available here.

pmma.title: Illuminated miniature building windows
pmma.use: Print a set of translucent windows for a lit architectural model.
pmma.why: PMMA's transparent-cover role suits small windows where light transmission and appearance dominate; ordinary FDM surface texture can diffuse the backlighting instead of requiring an optically polished result.
pmma.advantage: Light-transmitting window inserts can spread the backlighting across miniature rooms instead of creating opaque cutouts.
pmma.tradeoff: Available filament choices are limited, and the catalog gives no quantitative optical or mechanical performance.

pom.title: Small reduction gear
pom.use: Print a low-load prototype gear to evaluate tooth engagement.
pom.why: POM is a classic gear material, so it is relevant where a gear must combine rigidity with sliding contact; the catalog's mechanical values come from extruded stock and cannot size the printed teeth.
pom.advantage: An acetal gear provides a plausible sliding tooth-contact surface for low-load mechanism trials.
pom.tradeoff: POM filament availability and machine compatibility are unusually limited.

pom.title: Replaceable sliding carriage pad
pom.use: Print a sacrificial pad for a manually moved fixture carriage.
pom.why: The catalog identifies POM for bushings and sliding parts, making it worth evaluating at a sliding interface where a rigid wear surface is needed instead of a rubber pad.
pom.advantage: A purpose-made sliding contact surface can localize wear to a replaceable pad rather than the carriage body.
pom.tradeoff: Extruded-stock property values do not establish the wear life of FDM layers.

pom.title: Low-load shaft bushing
pom.use: Print a trial bushing for a hand-operated mechanism.
pom.why: POM's established bushing and bearing role makes it a candidate for guiding a slowly moving shaft; low water uptake in stock also motivates evaluating fit in varying humidity.
pom.advantage: A rigid bearing surface can guide the shaft while the low-water-uptake material reduces one source of fit change.
pom.tradeoff: Bore accuracy, friction and printed-layer wear need measurement rather than assuming machined-POM performance.

pom.title: Conveyor guide roller sleeve
pom.use: Print a replaceable sleeve for a small demonstration conveyor roller.
pom.why: POM is used for conveyor and sliding parts, so a roller sleeve is a practical way to explore its contact behavior while retaining a separate metal axle and bearing.
pom.advantage: A separate acetal contact sleeve concentrates conveyor contact on the replaceable part of the roller.
pom.tradeoff: Acids and oxidizing cleaners can attack POM, and filament grades may contain antistatic additives.

pom.title: Cam follower shoe
pom.use: Print a replaceable contact shoe for a low-speed mechanical cam prototype.
pom.why: The combination of a rigid acetal polymer and its established sliding-part applications makes a shaped follower surface plausible; the cam can push against a broad surface instead of a sharp printed edge.
pom.advantage: The shaped acetal contact surface can follow the cam while remaining replaceable as wear develops.
pom.tradeoff: Printed fatigue and contact-pressure limits are unknown, so verify wear and deformation experimentally.

pvdf.title: Chemical-bath basket insert
pvdf.use: Print an open basket for holding test coupons in a compatible laboratory bath.
pvdf.why: PVDF's resistance to many acids, solvents and oxidizing agents makes it a candidate for repeated wet exposure; its low water uptake helps avoid the swelling associated with more moisture-sensitive polymers.
pvdf.advantage: Resistance to the confirmed bath chemistry can help the basket survive repeated exposure without dissolving or swelling.
pvdf.tradeoff: Confirm the exact bath chemistry, especially strong alkalis, and do not assume an FDM basket is liquid-tight.

pvdf.title: Outdoor sensor cable clip
pvdf.use: Print a clip that positions a cable on an exposed test stand.
pvdf.why: PVDF combines strong UV and weather resistance with very low moisture uptake, giving a reason to evaluate it where rain and sunlight are continuous service conditions.
pvdf.advantage: Weather resistance can help the clip retain its role through repeated rain and sunlight exposure.
pvdf.tradeoff: PVDF requires expert processing and can warp; thin sections still need retention and creep testing.

pvdf.title: Solvent-transfer funnel
pvdf.use: Print an open funnel for a confirmed compatible laboratory solvent.
pvdf.why: PVDF's broad chemical resistance makes it relevant where ordinary decorative plastics may soften or crack; the open geometry avoids treating a porous printed part as a pressure vessel.
pvdf.advantage: Chemical resistance can keep the funnel usable with a confirmed compatible liquid that attacks less resistant plastics.
pvdf.tradeoff: Verify solvent compatibility and leakage, since several organic solvents swell or dissolve PVDF.

pvdf.title: Tank-top probe positioning bracket
pvdf.use: Print a bracket that holds a noncritical probe above a compatible chemical tank.
pvdf.why: Chemical resistance and low moisture uptake make PVDF attractive for splash exposure, while the bracket geometry can keep fasteners and adjustment features away from the wetted area.
pvdf.advantage: A chemically resistant mount can maintain probe position despite repeated compatible splashes around the tank.
pvdf.tradeoff: PVDF has substantial thermal expansion, so slots and fit checks are important when temperatures change.

pvdf.title: Outdoor tubing identification sleeve
pvdf.use: Print a slotted sleeve carrying raised identification text for an exposed tube.
pvdf.why: PVDF's weather resistance makes it a candidate when a label must remain outdoors, and chemical resistance can help where occasional compatible cleaning splashes reach the part.
pvdf.advantage: UV and weather resistance support longer outdoor identification service than a material selected only for indoor appearance.
pvdf.tradeoff: The sleeve should identify tubing rather than contain pressure; printing demands a controlled process window.

peek-cf.title: Stiff heated-fixture crossbar
peek-cf.use: Print a carbon-filled PEEK crossbar for a noncritical assembly fixture.
peek-cf.why: Carbon-filled PEEK has substantially higher printed in-plane modulus than unfilled PEEK, so it is a candidate when bending deflection matters more than large deformation or snap-fit toughness.
peek-cf.advantage: Higher bending stiffness can keep the verified crossbar and its locating points from deflecting as much under load.
peek-cf.tradeoff: Low elongation and layer dependence make impact and cross-layer loads important validation points.

peek-cf.title: Dimensional reference bracket
peek-cf.use: Print a rigid bracket that holds two noncritical fixture datums apart.
peek-cf.why: Fiber reinforcement raises stiffness and reduces thermal expansion in published stock data, motivating evaluation when relative spacing must stay stable as a fixture warms.
peek-cf.advantage: High stiffness and reduced expansion can help maintain datum spacing in a validated thermal fixture.
peek-cf.tradeoff: Stock expansion values are not a printed-part specification, and fiber direction can make printed movement uneven.

peek-cf.title: Lightweight gripper backbone
peek-cf.use: Print the rigid backbone of a small experimental robot gripper.
peek-cf.why: The carbon-filled grade's high in-plane stiffness makes it suitable to evaluate for a thin backbone that should bend little under load; compliant contact pads remain separate components.
peek-cf.advantage: A stiffer backbone can preserve finger alignment while separate compliant pads provide the contact cushioning.
peek-cf.tradeoff: Its low elongation makes it unsuitable to assume reliable spring fingers or resilient snap features.

peek-cf.title: Replaceable machining-fixture jaw body
peek-cf.use: Print a shaped jaw body for gentle holding trials in a benchtop fixture.
peek-cf.why: Published printed stiffness, together with creep data from extruded PEEK-CF stock, motivates evaluating a shaped jaw; the stock result does not establish printed creep performance.
peek-cf.advantage: If printed creep testing confirms stability, the stiff jaw could maintain workpiece position during a long dwell.
peek-cf.tradeoff: Qualify printed creep under the actual load, temperature and orientation; abrasive fiber-filled filament also requires suitable hardware.

peek-cf.title: Warm-process sensor mounting plate
peek-cf.use: Print a carbon-filled PEEK plate for positioning a noncritical process sensor.
peek-cf.why: Higher stiffness and published printed heat-deflection data give a reason to evaluate this grade where a thin mounting plate sees both heat and vibration-induced bending.
peek-cf.advantage: A stiff heat-capable mounting plate can help a validated sensor installation preserve its aim as the process warms.
peek-cf.tradeoff: Heat-deflection coupons do not define a continuous service temperature for this printed assembly.

pps-cf.title: Solvent-exposed fixture frame
pps-cf.use: Print a carbon-filled PPS frame for holding parts during compatible cleaning trials.
pps-cf.why: PPS chemistry provides broad solvent resistance, while carbon reinforcement raises printed stiffness so the frame can maintain spacing without very thick walls.
pps-cf.advantage: Solvent resistance and stiffness can help a verified frame maintain sample spacing through compatible cleaning trials.
pps-cf.tradeoff: The low printed elongation makes sharp corners and impact loads risky, and solvent resistance does not establish joint strength.

pps-cf.title: Heat-exposed inspection bracket
pps-cf.use: Print a rigid bracket for a noncritical inspection sensor near a warm process.
pps-cf.why: PPS-CF has published printed heat-deflection data and a relatively high modulus, giving a reason to evaluate it when both temperature and deflection matter.
pps-cf.advantage: Heat-capable stiffness can help the tested bracket preserve sensor alignment instead of drooping during warm operation.
pps-cf.tradeoff: HDT changes substantially with test load and is not a continuous-use rating for the finished part.

pps-cf.title: Low-moisture precision fixture nest
pps-cf.use: Print a nest that locates a component during indoor assembly.
pps-cf.why: The combination of low moisture absorption and high printed stiffness makes PPS-CF relevant when maintaining fixture dimensions matters more than resilient contact or snap action.
pps-cf.advantage: Low moisture uptake reduces one source of dimensional change while stiffness helps the nest resist clamping deflection.
pps-cf.tradeoff: The brittle grade needs generous radii and tested clamp forces rather than interference-fit retention.

pps-cf.title: Chemical-process cable guide
pps-cf.use: Print a rigid guide for routing cables near compatible cleaning splashes.
pps-cf.why: PPS resists many solvents and the fiber-filled grade is stiff, so a short guide can maintain a defined cable bend path in an environment that challenges ordinary plastics.
pps-cf.advantage: A chemically resistant rigid guide can keep cables separated during compatible cleaning exposure.
pps-cf.tradeoff: Sharp impacts can crack this low-elongation composite, and the specific chemicals still require compatibility checks.

pps-cf.title: Warm fixture spacer set
pps-cf.use: Print keyed spacers for a noncritical fixture that operates around heat.
pps-cf.why: PPS-CF offers high printed stiffness and published high heat-deflection results, motivating an evaluation where spacers must preserve alignment rather than flex.
pps-cf.advantage: High stiffness can help verified spacers retain the intended alignment under a modest warm fixture load.
pps-cf.tradeoff: Do not substitute the unfilled-stock continuous-service figure for a tested temperature limit on the carbon-filled printed spacers.

peek.title: Heat-exposed fixture locating block
peek.use: Print a locating block for a noncritical heated assembly fixture.
peek.why: PEEK combines rigidity with chemical resistance and published printed mechanical data, making it a candidate when a general-purpose plastic loses shape or is attacked during cleaning.
peek.advantage: Chemical and thermal resilience can help a verified fixture retain its locating function through process and cleaning exposure.
peek.tradeoff: The part's temperature and load limits must be validated; bulk service ratings do not establish FDM performance.

peek.title: Steam-cleaned laboratory sample rack
peek.use: Print a rack for organizing nonclinical laboratory samples through cleaning cycles.
peek.why: PEEK's resistance to water and steam makes repeated wet cleaning a meaningful reason to choose it, while a rigid lattice can hold differently shaped sample containers.
peek.advantage: Resistance to steam and water can support repeated cleaning without immediately requiring a new rack.
peek.tradeoff: A printed rack needs cycle testing for distortion and cleanliness; material resistance alone does not validate sterilization.

peek.title: Low-speed indexing wheel
peek.use: Print an indexing wheel for a benchtop mechanism exposed to compatible cleaning agents.
peek.why: Unfilled PEEK's printed elongation is substantially higher than the fiber-filled grade, making it worth considering when occasional impacts accompany a stiff mechanical function.
peek.advantage: Greater ductility than filled PEEK offers useful deformation margin during occasional low-energy knocks in a tested mechanism.
peek.tradeoff: Layer orientation strongly affects impact behavior, so do not size the wheel from in-plane tensile values alone.

peek.title: Chemical-test coupon holder
peek.use: Print a holder that keeps multiple test coupons separated in a compatible exposure setup.
peek.why: PEEK's broad solvent resistance supports use around many chemicals, while its rigid structure allows repeatable coupon spacing and a removable handling feature.
peek.advantage: Chemical resistance can preserve the holder during compatible exposures so sample spacing remains repeatable between trials.
peek.tradeoff: Concentrated acids can attack PEEK, and the actual chemistry and printed strength require verification.

peek.title: Repeated-use assembly flexure prototype
peek.use: Print a generously radiused flexure for a low-load benchtop assembly experiment.
peek.why: PEEK has published fatigue advantages and comparatively ductile printed in-plane behavior, giving a reason to evaluate it when a rigid plastic element must bend repeatedly by a small amount.
peek.advantage: Fatigue resistance makes repeated low-strain motion a meaningful goal for a carefully tested integral flexure.
peek.tradeoff: No catalog fatigue curve qualifies a particular printed flexure; orientation, strain and cycle life need testing.

pei-1010.title: Heated assembly positioning nest
pei-1010.use: Print a positioning nest for a noncritical heated assembly process.
pei-1010.why: ULTEM 1010 has higher printed heat-deflection results than 9085 in this catalog, so it is a candidate when fixture rigidity during heat exposure drives material selection.
pei-1010.advantage: The grade's thermal rigidity can help a tested nest maintain locating contact during a warm assembly step.
pei-1010.tradeoff: Coupon HDT does not establish the fixture's working temperature, and cross-layer strength is considerably lower.

pei-1010.title: Thermal-test cable comb
pei-1010.use: Print a cable comb that spaces test leads inside a warm experimental chamber.
pei-1010.why: PEI 1010 combines rigidity with comparatively high printed heat-deflection performance, making it useful to evaluate where a simple cable separator must retain its geometry.
pei-1010.advantage: Heat-capable rigidity can preserve cable spacing without relying on flexing clip arms during the thermal trial.
pei-1010.tradeoff: Brittleness favors open slots and screw retention over repeatedly flexed snap closures.

pei-1010.title: Heat-cleaned tooling tray
pei-1010.use: Print a partitioned tray for reusable nonclinical laboratory tooling.
pei-1010.why: PEI 1010 is identified for autoclavable tooling, giving a reason to evaluate it when repeated hot cleaning is part of the workflow rather than ordinary room-temperature storage.
pei-1010.advantage: Hot-cleaning capability can extend tray reuse when the actual printed geometry survives the validated cleaning cycle.
pei-1010.tradeoff: Validate the printed tray's cleaning cycle, deformation and surface condition; resin descriptions do not certify cleanliness or sterilization.

pei-1010.title: Warm fixture datum block
pei-1010.use: Print a thick datum block for a noncritical temperature-cycling fixture.
pei-1010.why: High printed modulus and heat-deflection results support considering PEI 1010 for a stable locating feature, while printed thermal-expansion data helps plan clearances.
pei-1010.advantage: A tested rigid block can preserve the fixture's locating geometry more effectively during a controlled temperature change.
pei-1010.tradeoff: Thermal expansion is orientation-dependent, and concentrated loads across layers require testing.

pei-1010.title: Heated bonding alignment jig
pei-1010.use: Print a jig that aligns parts during a trial adhesive cure.
pei-1010.why: PEI 1010's heat-deflection performance makes it a candidate for warm tooling, while its rigid geometry can keep several mating surfaces positioned simultaneously.
pei-1010.advantage: Heat-capable rigidity can keep mating parts aligned throughout a validated warm adhesive-cure step.
pei-1010.tradeoff: Check adhesive and cleaning compatibility because ketones and aromatic solvents can craze PEI; no cure temperature follows automatically from HDT.

pei-9085.title: Interior ventilation-duct prototype
pei-9085.use: Print a noninstalled duct prototype for evaluating an interior airflow layout.
pei-9085.why: ULTEM 9085 has published flame, smoke and toxicity test data that makes it relevant when investigating interior-material requirements, while its rigidity supports complex duct shapes.
pei-9085.advantage: The documented material test pedigree gives engineers relevant evidence when selecting candidates for later duct qualification.
pei-9085.tradeoff: Material test pedigree does not approve an installed duct; final part geometry and process need their own qualification.

pei-9085.title: Equipment-console panel prototype
pei-9085.use: Print a panel that checks the fit of switches and display openings.
pei-9085.why: PEI 9085 combines documented interior-material fire-test information with printed strength data, making it a candidate when the prototype should explore more than cosmetic appearance.
pei-9085.advantage: The grade's documented interior-material test information can support a more informed material-screening stage for the panel.
pei-9085.tradeoff: Its thermal ceiling differs from PEI 1010, and neither resin ratings nor catalog coupons certify the panel.

pei-9085.title: Warm instrumentation mounting bracket
pei-9085.use: Print a bracket for a noncritical laboratory instrument near heat.
pei-9085.why: Published printed tensile retention at elevated temperatures gives a reason to consider 9085 when a bracket must keep carrying a modest load as it warms.
pei-9085.advantage: Elevated-temperature strength retention can help a tested bracket keep the instrument aligned as its surroundings warm.
pei-9085.tradeoff: In-plane and cross-layer behavior differ, so elevated-temperature coupon data cannot set the assembly's allowable load.

pei-9085.title: Sun-exposed enclosure mounting frame
pei-9085.use: Print a frame for evaluating a sensor enclosure on an outdoor test stand.
pei-9085.why: Published weathering results show useful strength retention for a tested 9085 print condition, making outdoor evaluation more grounded than choosing solely by resin family.
pei-9085.advantage: The reported strength retention after weathering supports evaluating longer exposure than an indoor-only material selection.
pei-9085.tradeoff: The accelerated-weathering result is not a service-life prediction, and color shift and bolt stresses still matter.

pei-9085.title: Interior cable-routing tray prototype
pei-9085.use: Print a tray for checking cable routing in a compact equipment mockup.
pei-9085.why: The material's interior-use fire-test pedigree and rigid printed structure make it relevant where cable routing must eventually satisfy defined material requirements.
pei-9085.advantage: The grade's interior-material test pedigree supports informed evaluation of a tray intended for later compliance testing.
pei-9085.tradeoff: Printed tray compliance requires application-specific testing, and the brittle structure should not rely on repeatedly flexed clips.

pekk.title: Complex heated-fixture bracket
pekk.use: Print an unfilled amorphous PEKK bracket for a noncritical thermal fixture.
pekk.why: Amorphous PEKK avoids PEEK's crystallization-control problem, making it attractive when a complex shape needs the PAEK family's properties but process control is a major concern.
pekk.advantage: Reduced crystallization-control demands can make a complex PAEK fixture more manageable to produce consistently on suitable equipment.
pekk.tradeoff: It still needs industrial high-temperature printing, and carbon-filled PEKK figures do not describe the unfilled part.

pekk.title: Solvent-cleaned assembly nest
pekk.use: Print an unfilled PEKK nest that holds a component during compatible solvent cleaning.
pekk.why: The catalog's chemical-compatibility information makes PEKK relevant where common organic cleaning solvents attack other plastics; a rigid nest can maintain repeatable component spacing.
pekk.advantage: Resistance to compatible organic solvents can preserve locating surfaces through repeated assembly-cleaning cycles.
pekk.tradeoff: Confirm the exact chemical and printed integrity, especially with concentrated acids; the nest is not a sealed chemical vessel.

pekk.title: Low-voltage insulating fixture spacer
pekk.use: Print an unfilled PEKK spacer for a noncritical low-voltage benchtop fixture.
pekk.why: The catalog identifies unfilled PEKK as electrically insulating, so it is a candidate when separation and a rigid complex shape are both required.
pekk.advantage: The unfilled insulating grade can separate conductive fixture components without adding a deliberately dissipative material path.
pekk.tradeoff: Carbon-filled and ESD PEKK grades behave differently, and insulation of a printed assembly needs appropriate testing.

pekk.title: Stiff gripper mounting plate
pekk.use: Print a carbon-filled PEKK plate for an experimental robot gripper.
pekk.why: The named CF15 grade has much higher printed modulus than unfilled PEKK, making it relevant when a mounting plate should resist bending under modest loads.
pekk.advantage: High CF-grade stiffness can help the tested gripper preserve alignment under bending loads.
pekk.tradeoff: The carbon-filled grade has low elongation and requires abrasion-resistant printing hardware; its numbers cannot be assigned to unfilled PEKK.

pekk.title: Temperature-cycling alignment comb
pekk.use: Print an unfilled PEKK comb that positions several test coupons.
pekk.why: Published printed expansion and elevated-temperature strength-retention data provide a basis for evaluating PEKK when coupon spacing must remain predictable during a controlled thermal experiment.
pekk.advantage: Known printed expansion behavior helps plan clearances so coupon positioning remains useful during the tested thermal cycle.
pekk.tradeoff: Expansion differs by print direction, and the fixture's allowable temperature and load require direct validation.

pps.title: Solvent-cleaning coupon rack
pps.use: Print an unfilled PPS rack for compatible chemical-exposure experiments.
pps.why: PPS's broad solvent resistance makes it a candidate when a fixture must tolerate cleaning chemicals, while its rigid geometry can keep multiple samples separated.
pps.advantage: Resistance to compatible solvents can preserve the rack for repeated exposures without requiring a disposable support fixture.
pps.tradeoff: Printed PPS heat-deflection data is much lower than some stock figures, so chemical resistance does not justify hot loaded service.

pps.title: Humidity-stable assembly spacer
pps.use: Print a spacer for an indoor assembly fixture exposed to changing humidity.
pps.why: Unfilled PPS has very low moisture absorption, making it relevant when changes in absorbed water could disturb a close fit or alignment.
pps.advantage: Low moisture uptake reduces one source of fit drift as the assembly environment becomes more humid.
pps.tradeoff: Measured dimensions and load response remain print-dependent; low moisture uptake alone does not guarantee precision or long-term stability.

pps.title: Cleaning-line sensor splash shield
pps.use: Print an open shield around a noncritical sensor mount.
pps.why: PPS chemistry is resistant to many solvents, so a rigid splash shield can be worth evaluating where cleaning overspray attacks ordinary enclosure plastics.
pps.advantage: A chemically resistant shield can continue redirecting compatible cleaning splashes without softening like a less suitable plastic.
pps.tradeoff: The shield is not chemical containment, and exposure conditions and exact solvent compatibility still require confirmation.

pps.title: Warm fixture alignment rail
pps.use: Print an unfilled PPS rail for noncritical positioning trials.
pps.why: PPS suppliers describe strong creep resistance, motivating its evaluation when a rail must maintain alignment under a sustained modest load rather than repeated large flexing.
pps.advantage: Creep resistance makes sustained alignment a meaningful target for the tested rail under a modest long-duration load.
pps.tradeoff: Those supplier claims include stock data; printed deflection and temperature capability need their own measurements.

pps.title: Chemical-bath tubing separator
pps.use: Print a slotted separator that keeps compatible laboratory tubes apart.
pps.why: PPS combines broad chemical resistance with minimal water absorption, providing a reason to evaluate it for repeated splash or immersion exposure in a confirmed compatible setup.
pps.advantage: Low water uptake and chemical resistance can help a verified separator retain useful tube spacing between wet cycles.
pps.tradeoff: This printed part should guide tubes rather than act as a pressure fitting, and concentrated joint stresses need testing.

ppsu.title: Steam-cleaned laboratory instrument tray
ppsu.use: Print a tray for reusable nonclinical laboratory tools.
ppsu.why: PPSU's resistance to repeated steam autoclaving is a specific reason to choose it over PSU when repeated hot wet cleaning is central to the workflow.
ppsu.advantage: Repeated-steam resistance can support tray reuse through a verified hot-cleaning routine instead of discarding it after each cycle.
ppsu.tradeoff: Printed PPSU is much less ductile than stock; the tray's cleaning durability and cleanliness must be validated directly.

ppsu.title: Washable sample-bottle carrier
ppsu.use: Print a carrier for sealed laboratory sample bottles.
ppsu.why: Repeated steam-cleaning resistance and published printed mechanical data make PPSU relevant when a carrier sees frequent cleaning rather than serving as a disposable organizer.
ppsu.advantage: Steam-resistant material can support repeated cleaning while the tested carrier keeps bottle positions organized.
ppsu.tradeoff: The carrier should not be assumed sterile, food-safe or impact-proof, and thin handles need printed strength testing.

ppsu.title: Automotive-fluid test fixture holder
ppsu.use: Print a holder for coupons used in noncritical automotive-fluid compatibility experiments.
ppsu.why: Published PPSF stress-crack tests include several automotive fluids, giving a concrete reason to evaluate PPSU around those specific exposures rather than assuming all sulfone polymers behave alike.
ppsu.advantage: Resistance to the verified automotive fluids can preserve sample positioning throughout a compatibility experiment.
ppsu.tradeoff: Passing published exposures does not establish indefinite compatibility or the printed holder's allowable load.

ppsu.title: Heat-cleaned tweezers positioning block
ppsu.use: Print a block that holds laboratory tweezers in separate open slots.
ppsu.why: PPSU's steam-cleaning resistance makes it a candidate when an organizer repeatedly enters a hot wet cleaning process and must retain its shape.
ppsu.advantage: Hot wet cleaning resistance can keep a verified organizer useful through repeated cleaning of the tool collection.
ppsu.tradeoff: The catalog's stock ductility is not representative of printed PPSU, so avoid tight snap fits and validate thermal cycling.

ppsu.title: Low-voltage warm-environment terminal spacer
ppsu.use: Print a spacer for a noncritical low-voltage test terminal assembly.
ppsu.why: Published printed PPSF electrical insulation and heat-deflection data give a reason to evaluate PPSU when a spacer must combine physical separation with heat exposure.
ppsu.advantage: Electrical insulation and heat-capable rigidity can help maintain physical terminal separation in a validated low-voltage fixture.
ppsu.tradeoff: FDM voids, humidity and geometry affect insulation; catalog coupon data cannot qualify the assembly or determine its temperature limit.

psu.title: Warm instrument housing prototype
psu.use: Print a housing to evaluate a low-voltage laboratory instrument around moderate heat.
psu.why: PSU is identified for high-temperature housings and has published printed heat-deflection data, so it is a candidate when ordinary plastics lose shape during a controlled trial.
psu.advantage: Heat-capable rigidity can help a validated housing keep connectors and internal components positioned during a warm trial.
psu.tradeoff: Its thermal capability is below PPSU, and the printed housing needs direct load and temperature validation.

psu.title: Hot-water experiment hose bracket
psu.use: Print a bracket that positions flexible tubing in a benchtop hot-water experiment.
psu.why: PSU's documented hot-water-fitting application makes it relevant to evaluate for external tube positioning without relying on the print to contain pressure.
psu.advantage: A verified PSU bracket can maintain tube routing through a warm experiment without serving as a pressure boundary.
psu.tradeoff: Do not transfer bulk service figures to the print, and test cleaning chemicals because ketones and aromatic solvents can craze PSU.

psu.title: Warm low-voltage connector standoff
psu.use: Print a standoff for a noncritical connector evaluation fixture.
psu.why: PSU combines an insulating material classification with rigidity and printed heat-deflection data, giving a reason to consider it when a shaped spacer must separate warm components.
psu.advantage: An insulating rigid spacer can maintain connector separation while tolerating the validated fixture's heat exposure.
psu.tradeoff: Surface-resistance data does not certify printed dielectric performance, and PSU is not a substitute for PPSU in repeated steam cycles.

psu.title: Temperature-test sample tray
psu.use: Print a tray that keeps small nonclinical samples separated during thermal experiments.
psu.why: The catalog identifies PSU for trays and gives printed mechanical and thermal data, making it a candidate when room-temperature organizers are too soft for a controlled trial.
psu.advantage: Heat-capable stiffness can keep the tested sample compartments separated and level through a thermal trial.
psu.tradeoff: A coupon HDT is not a working-temperature specification, and the tray must be tested under its actual sample load.

psu.title: Solvent-free warm assembly fixture
psu.use: Print a fixture that holds parts during a dry warm assembly step.
psu.why: PSU's rigidity and published printed heat-deflection data make it relevant where a fixture sees heat but does not need PPSU's repeated-steam capability.
psu.advantage: Thermal rigidity can help a verified fixture preserve assembly alignment throughout the warm process step.
psu.tradeoff: Ketones, esters and aromatic cleaners can attack PSU, so the assembly and cleaning workflow must be compatible.

sup-breakaway.title: PLA console underside support
sup-breakaway.use: Print PolySupport for PLA beneath the accessible underside of a PLA console mockup.
sup-breakaway.why: A matched breakaway interface supports the broad overhang while remaining mechanically removable, so the console body stays PLA and the support is discarded.
sup-breakaway.advantage: Mechanical removal avoids a dissolution delay while supporting a cleaner, less drooping PLA overhang during printing.
sup-breakaway.tradeoff: This pairing is grade-specific, and removing support from thin PLA edges can still damage them.

sup-breakaway.title: PLA figurine arm support
sup-breakaway.use: Print matched PLA breakaway support under an outstretched arm and its fingertips.
sup-breakaway.why: The separate support material can sustain the overhang without making the model itself from a weak sacrificial polymer; open access lets the support be removed by hand.
sup-breakaway.advantage: A separable interface can reduce the force needed to free the arm compared with a fused model-material support.
sup-breakaway.tradeoff: Fragile fingers need cautious removal and a tuned interface rather than aggressive pulling.

sup-breakaway.title: PA12 bracket counterbore support
sup-breakaway.use: Print PolySupport for PA12 inside an accessible downward-facing bolt recess.
sup-breakaway.why: The PA12-specific support grade is matched to nylon processing and adhesion, allowing the recess roof to print while the bracket remains PA12.
sup-breakaway.advantage: The matched removable interface supports the bolt recess while reducing the need to force apart fused PA12 support contacts.
sup-breakaway.tradeoff: Confirm the exact PA12 pairing; PLA breakaway support is a different formulation and inaccessible pockets cannot be peeled cleanly.

sup-breakaway.title: PA12 duct flange support
sup-breakaway.use: Print PA12-matched breakaway support beneath the outer lip of an open duct flange.
sup-breakaway.why: A removable interface supports the wide lip while leaving the model body in nylon, and the open flange edge provides a route for mechanical removal.
sup-breakaway.advantage: A matched peel-away interface can support the flange lip while leaving a practical removal route at its open edge.
sup-breakaway.tradeoff: Peel-away support cannot clear a sealed internal passage, and the material-specific adhesion must be tuned.

sup-breakaway.title: PLA enclosure latch recess support
sup-breakaway.use: Print matched PLA breakaway support below an exposed recess beside an enclosure latch.
sup-breakaway.why: The support carries the recess roof during printing and then peels away from an opening large enough for access, preserving the PLA latch geometry.
sup-breakaway.advantage: A matched removable interface supports the recess roof while avoiding a water-dissolution stage before enclosure assembly.
sup-breakaway.tradeoff: Avoid trapping support behind the latch, and test the interface because a brittle model edge can chip during removal.

bvoh.title: PLA articulated mechanism gap support
bvoh.use: Print BVOH in reachable gaps around a PLA demonstration linkage.
bvoh.why: Water-soluble support can be removed from gaps that are awkward to peel, while the linkage remains PLA; Fiberlogy explicitly lists PLA among compatible model materials.
bvoh.advantage: Water removal can release supported linkage gaps without levering a rigid support against the mechanism.
bvoh.tradeoff: Provide water access and drainage to every supported gap, and keep the highly moisture-sensitive spool dry.

bvoh.title: PETG curved internal channel support
bvoh.use: Print BVOH beneath the roof of an open-ended PETG demonstration channel.
bvoh.why: Fiberlogy lists PET-G compatibility, and dissolution can remove support along a curved channel where pliers cannot reach; the channel body remains PETG.
bvoh.advantage: Dissolution can clear support from the curved passage where straight mechanical tools cannot reach.
bvoh.tradeoff: Water must circulate through the entire channel, and small openings can greatly prolong removal.

bvoh.title: ABS recessed impeller blade support
bvoh.use: Print BVOH under the blades of an ABS display impeller.
bvoh.why: Fiberlogy names ABS compatibility, making water-removable support worth evaluating beneath blades with narrow access; ABS forms the finished object and BVOH is discarded.
bvoh.advantage: Water removal can clear blade recesses without forcing each support contact against a thin ABS edge.
bvoh.tradeoff: The two-material temperature and adhesion settings need testing, and the soluble filament must stay dry.

bvoh.title: ASA duct elbow roof support
bvoh.use: Print BVOH below the interior roof of an open-ended ASA duct prototype.
bvoh.why: Fiberlogy lists ASA compatibility, and dissolvable support offers a route to removing material beyond a straight mechanical reach while leaving the ASA duct intact.
bvoh.advantage: Dissolution can clear the curved duct interior while preserving a continuous ASA shell for geometry trials.
bvoh.tradeoff: This does not establish airtightness, and the water bath needs access to both ends.

bvoh.title: PLA lattice display support
bvoh.use: Print BVOH under shallow overhangs inside an open PLA lattice sculpture.
bvoh.why: Water dissolution makes it possible to remove support from the lattice without snapping each narrow support contact by hand; PLA is an explicitly listed compatible model polymer.
bvoh.advantage: Water removal can free many delicate lattice openings without breaking each rigid support contact by hand.
bvoh.tradeoff: BVOH is costly and moisture-sensitive, so interface-only use and dry feeding may matter for an economical trial.

sup-soluble-ht.title: PC enclosure ledge support
sup-soluble-ht.use: Print THERMAX MTS1 beneath an accessible ledge in a PC enclosure prototype.
sup-soluble-ht.why: MTS1 is the catalog's PC and PC/ABS-matched breakaway grade, so it can support an overhang without using ordinary low-temperature PLA or PVA supports.
sup-soluble-ht.advantage: The matched support survives the relevant hot build while providing a separable interface beneath the PC ledge.
sup-soluble-ht.tradeoff: This grade is mechanically removed; it is not a water-soluble material and needs a reachable removal path.

sup-soluble-ht.title: PC/ABS bracket recess support
sup-soluble-ht.use: Print MTS1 under the roof of an open PC/ABS bracket pocket.
sup-soluble-ht.why: The model polymer pairing is explicitly identified in the catalog, and the support is formulated for hotter engineering-material processing than ordinary PLA-oriented support.
sup-soluble-ht.advantage: Hot-process compatibility and mechanical separability can produce a supported PC/ABS pocket roof with practical removal access.
sup-soluble-ht.tradeoff: Tune the interface and leave tool access, because breakaway support trapped inside a closed pocket cannot dissolve in water.

sup-soluble-ht.title: PEEK open duct flange support
sup-soluble-ht.use: Print a matched THERMAX high-temperature breakaway support under an exposed PEEK flange.
sup-soluble-ht.why: The high-temperature support class is intended to survive PAEK build conditions that ordinary PVA or PLA support cannot, while the finished duct remains PEEK.
sup-soluble-ht.advantage: Heat-resistant support can remain functional during the PEEK build instead of degrading like a low-temperature support.
sup-soluble-ht.tradeoff: Confirm the exact support grade and chamber limits, and provide mechanical removal access.

sup-soluble-ht.title: PEI fixture overhang support
sup-soluble-ht.use: Print a matched THERMAX high-temperature breakaway grade beneath an exposed PEI fixture arm.
sup-soluble-ht.why: This support class is paired with PEI and formulated for high-temperature builds, giving the projecting arm a temporary foundation without changing the fixture's model material.
sup-soluble-ht.advantage: Heat-resistant support can carry the overhang through the PEI build while preserving an accessible separable interface.
sup-soluble-ht.tradeoff: Grade matching and dual-extruder process tuning are necessary, and high-temperature support does not imply water solubility.

sup-soluble-ht.title: PPSU curved channel sacrificial support
sup-soluble-ht.use: Print IEMAI HT-SP in an open-ended PPSU demonstration channel.
sup-soluble-ht.why: The catalog lists HT-SP for PPSU and specifies alkaline dissolution, offering a different removal route when internal curvature prevents peeling a breakaway support from the channel.
sup-soluble-ht.advantage: Alkaline dissolution can clear an internal curve that would trap a mechanically removed high-temperature support.
sup-soluble-ht.tradeoff: HT-SP is not plain-water soluble; confirm bath compatibility, access and the manufacturer's processing instructions before using it.

pva.title: Drying Elephant dish-rack support
pva.use: Use PVA as sacrificial support for the creator's Drying Elephant dish rack.
pva.why: The documented build used Orbi-tech PVA support and dissolved it in cold water overnight; PVA supports the geometry temporarily rather than forming the elephant's finished model body.
pva.advantage: Water dissolution clears sacrificial support while preserving the finished model body rather than forcing support away mechanically.
pva.tradeoff: That creator result is grade-specific, and the moisture-sensitive filament needs dry storage and feeding.

pva.title: PLA ball-in-cage display support
pva.use: Print PolyDissolve S1 around the lower surfaces of a PLA ball inside an open cage.
pva.why: The catalog pairs this PVA grade with PLA, and water dissolution can clear support through the cage openings without forcing the ball out.
pva.advantage: Dissolution can free the captive ball without prying apart the open PLA cage around it.
pva.tradeoff: Every support region needs water access, and dimensional clearances still require tuning.

pva.title: TPU curved grip-channel support
pva.use: Print PolyDissolve S1 beneath an overhanging channel in a TPU grip prototype.
pva.why: The catalog explicitly pairs this grade with TPU, and dissolving support avoids pulling hard mechanical support against a flexible channel wall.
pva.advantage: Water removal can release the supported recess without pulling stiff support against the flexible TPU wall.
pva.tradeoff: Adhesion, feed behavior and drying need testing; soft TPU does not automatically make a multi-material print reliable.

pva.title: PETG open-ended manifold model support
pva.use: Print PolyDissolve S1 under the roof of an open-ended PETG flow-path model.
pva.why: Its documented PETG pairing and water solubility make PVA relevant where a curved interior is difficult to reach with tools; PETG forms the final body.
pva.advantage: Dissolution can clear support from the curved PETG passage through its flushing openings.
pva.tradeoff: Maintain flushing openings and validate drainage; this example does not establish pressure-tightness or suitability as a working fluid manifold.

pva.title: PVB architectural arch support
pva.use: Print PolyDissolve S1 under the deep arches of a PVB architectural model.
pva.why: PVB is one of this grade's explicitly named pairings, and dissolving PVA can remove material behind decorative columns without prying against delicate surfaces.
pva.advantage: Water dissolution can clear support behind delicate PVB columns without levering against the facade.
pva.tradeoff: Remove PVA with water before any finishing trials; alcohol or acetone alone does not dissolve the support.

conductive.title: OpenPrintSense finger-bend sensor glove
conductive.use: Sense finger motion using a printed conductive element on a separate flexible support.
conductive.why: The existing build reports Recreus Conductive Filaflex, a conductive TPU; flexibility and conductivity belong to that product rather than rigid conductive PLA.
conductive.advantage: The selected conductive TPU can follow finger motion while supplying a sensing element, avoiding the rigidity of a conductive PLA strip.
conductive.tradeoff: Sensor response and durability need calibration, and this is not a medical measurement device.

conductive.title: Capacitive touch-button insert
conductive.use: Create a shaped touch electrode connected to an external sensing circuit.
conductive.why: A conductive carbon-filled filament can form the electrode itself, making it useful where a custom curved touch surface is wanted.
conductive.advantage: Conductivity throughout the printed shape lets the touch surface act as an electrode without adding a separate metal face.
conductive.tradeoff: Measure resistance and contact reliability; a conductive print is not equivalent to copper wiring.

conductive.title: Low-current continuity teaching model
conductive.use: Demonstrate a simple conducting path in a classroom circuit experiment.
conductive.why: The conductive composite allows a visibly three-dimensional path to carry a small signal, making geometry and electrical behavior easy to discuss together.
conductive.advantage: The printed polymer itself conducts the test signal, letting students compare electrical paths made from different three-dimensional geometries.
conductive.tradeoff: Keep it to suitable low-current experiments and verify resistance rather than treating it as a power conductor.

conductive.title: Custom capacitive slider electrode
conductive.use: Print a shaped electrode behind a separate insulating control surface.
conductive.why: Conductive filament supports an electrode geometry that follows an unusual housing, useful for exploratory touch-interface prototypes.
conductive.advantage: The conductive printed shape can serve directly as the slider electrode, avoiding a separately formed metal electrode inside the curved housing.
conductive.tradeoff: Touch performance depends on the complete circuit, geometry and grounding, so the finished assembly needs tuning.

conductive.title: Compliant pressure-button prototype
conductive.use: Make a deformable conductive button for a low-current interactive experiment.
conductive.why: Select a conductive TPU product such as Filaflex rather than the brittle PLA-based grades when deformation is part of the function.
conductive.advantage: The same custom geometry can supply compliance and an electrical sensing element.
conductive.tradeoff: Resistance changes, contact behavior and repeated-use life must be measured for the actual printed button.

magnetic.title: Magnet-retained display token
magnetic.use: Make an iron-filled token that can be held by an existing magnet.
magnetic.why: Ferromagnetic powder makes the print respond to magnets, allowing a custom token shape without embedding a steel insert.
magnetic.advantage: The decorative part can attach directly to a magnetic holder.
magnetic.tradeoff: It is not a permanent magnet, and retention force needs testing because the iron is diluted by PLA.

magnetic.title: Removable magnetic-fixture locator
magnetic.use: Produce a lightweight locator block held against a magnet-equipped fixture.
magnetic.why: Iron-filled PLA is useful when the printed shape needs to be attracted by the fixture’s magnets rather than provide magnetic force itself.
magnetic.advantage: Attraction from the embedded iron lets a custom locator attach to existing magnets without adding a separate steel mounting plate.
magnetic.tradeoff: Treat the magnet as retention only after checking force, and avoid heavily loaded or impact-sensitive locations.

magnetic.title: Rust-finished theatrical relic
magnetic.use: Create a decorative prop intended to acquire a real rusty surface.
magnetic.why: Exposed iron powder can oxidize, so this formulation offers a weathered finish that ordinary metallic-colored PLA cannot reproduce by itself.
magnetic.advantage: The finish can follow intricate printed textures without fabricating a metal object.
magnetic.tradeoff: The rusting behavior is a decorative feature rather than corrosion resistance, and staining adjacent materials is possible.

magnetic.title: Magnetic-response classroom model
magnetic.use: Demonstrate how an iron-filled printed object responds to an external magnet.
magnetic.why: The composite’s ferromagnetic behavior makes it useful for comparing ordinary polymer and iron-loaded parts with the same shape.
magnetic.advantage: Magnetic attraction becomes visible in a shape normally associated with plastic, helping isolate the effect of the iron filler.
magnetic.tradeoff: Do not infer pure-iron magnetic performance or electrical conductivity from attraction alone.

magnetic.title: Magnet-held sculptural panel accent
magnetic.use: Add a removable decorative relief to an indoor display with hidden magnets.
magnetic.why: The iron-loaded composite combines a printable relief surface with attraction to magnets, and it can also be polished or deliberately rusted.
magnetic.advantage: The iron-filled relief can attach to hidden magnets without a separate metal backing plate on the decorative part.
magnetic.tradeoff: The dense, brittle print needs sufficient magnetic support and protection from accidental knocks.

pvb.title: Alcohol-smoothed display figurine
pvb.use: Produce an indoor figurine whose visible surface receives controlled IPA smoothing.
pvb.why: A smoothable PVB grade such as PolySmooth is selected because isopropyl alcohol can reduce visible layer texture.
pvb.advantage: A complex curved model can gain a more uniform finish without sanding every recess.
pvb.tradeoff: Smoothing can round fine details, and IPA use requires appropriate handling rather than an assumption of harmless vapour.

pvb.title: Translucent decorative light cover
pvb.use: Make a cosmetic cover for a cool, low-power light source.
pvb.why: A suitable translucent PVB grade can be alcohol-smoothed to reduce the strongly layered appearance of its outer surface.
pvb.advantage: The cover can combine a complex printed form with a smoother visual finish.
pvb.tradeoff: Validate light diffusion and temperature in the actual assembly; smoothing does not establish optical quality or heat safety.

pvb.title: Product presentation housing
pvb.use: Show the external form of a new device in a polished visual prototype.
pvb.why: PVB’s alcohol-smoothable surface suits appearance evaluation where a visible extrusion texture would distract from the shape.
pvb.advantage: A more uniform surface helps assess curves and reflections before making production tooling.
pvb.tradeoff: It is a presentation model, and smoothing does not qualify its fit or mechanical performance.

pvb.title: Investment-casting pattern in PolyCast
pvb.use: Create a sacrificial printed pattern for an investment-casting workflow.
pvb.why: Choose the purpose-formulated PolyCast grade: its clean-burnout behavior is the relevant feature, rather than assuming every PVB product behaves identically.
pvb.advantage: The dedicated casting grade is intended to burn out cleanly, reducing the concern about ordinary filament residue in the investment mold.
pvb.tradeoff: The casting process still needs a validated burnout schedule and suitable professional equipment.

pvb.title: Smooth decorative architectural model
pvb.use: Represent curved architectural surfaces in an indoor presentation model.
pvb.why: A smoothable PVB grade can reduce layer texture on forms that are awkward to sand by hand.
pvb.advantage: The finished model can emphasize the intended geometry and reflected light more clearly.
pvb.tradeoff: PVB is highly moisture sensitive, so dry storage and preparation are important for clean printing.

peba.title: Airless bouncy ball
peba.use: The documented Bouncy Balls design was developed and tested with 90A PEBA.
peba.why: The creator reports strong bounce for PEBA and much less bounce from their TPU trials; PEBA's flexible block structure and high printed elongation are consistent with exploring resilient lattice geometries.
peba.advantage: The documented PEBA lattice provides strong bounce in the creator's trials without an inflatable bladder.
peba.tradeoff: The reported bounce applies to this design and settings, not every PEBA print or a standardized rebound comparison.

peba.title: Footwear heel-lattice test section
peba.use: Print a small heel-shaped lattice to compare footwear prototype geometries.
peba.why: PEBA combines a flexible block-polymer structure with large printed elongation, and the manufacturer explicitly lists footwear and cushioning among its applications, supporting evaluation of compressible lattice sections.
peba.advantage: The compliant lattice can explore compressible support with the low-density PEBA grade rather than a rigid material.
peba.tradeoff: Neither elongation nor nominal 90A hardness establishes comfort, energy return or fatigue life; test the actual geometry under cyclic compression.

peba.title: Experimental rebound wheel ring
peba.use: Fit a compliant PEBA ring to a small indoor rolling demonstrator.
peba.why: The flexible block structure and high elongation support evaluating an elastically deforming ring, with the documented ball example suggesting rebound is worth investigating rather than assuming TPU-equivalent behavior.
peba.advantage: The deformable ring can explore elastic recovery while its rigid hub preserves the axle interface.
peba.tradeoff: There is no wheel traction or wear measurement here, and the lower printed Z strength makes layer orientation consequential.

peba.title: Compliant sports-grip prototype sleeve
peba.use: Create a removable PEBA sleeve for a noncritical sports-equipment grip prototype.
peba.why: The manufacturer lists sports equipment as an application, while the nominal 90A grade and high printed elongation support a deformable sleeve that can stretch around a shaped core.
peba.advantage: The flexible sleeve can stretch onto a core and provide a deformable hand-contact layer over it.
peba.tradeoff: The catalog does not establish sweat compatibility, grip friction or long-term retention; test those properties on the selected grade.

peba.title: Returning flexure demonstration element
peba.use: Print a replaceable flexible element for a guarded hand-operated mechanism demonstration.
peba.why: PEBA's rigid and flexible blocks and large printed elongation make it a candidate for exploring reversible deformation through curved flexure geometry, rather than treating it as a rigid structural polymer.
peba.advantage: The flexible element can permit mechanism travel without requiring a separate pin joint at its center.
peba.tradeoff: Elongation at break does not establish elastic working strain or fatigue life, and layer orientation affects the weaker Z direction.
